notes.title: Denial rate — Q1
notes.content:
9.2% initial denial rate, down from 11.4%. Overturn rate on appeal 61%.

The improvement is documentation quality, which is interesting given there is a documentation pilot running on two units. I have not claimed the connection because two units is not a sample and the timing could be coincidence.

notes.title: Payer — Meridian Health Plan, contract performance
notes.content:
Their denial rate against us runs three points above the book. Most of it is one edit rule on a common medical-surgical code.

I have raised it twice with their network manager. Their position is that the rule is standard; mine is that nobody else applies it this way. This is a contract conversation, not a claims conversation, and I keep having it at the claims level.

notes.title: Why claims are PHI
notes.content:
Every conversation with a finance person starts here.

A claim carries a patient, a diagnosis code, a service date, and a provider. Putting it in a spreadsheet does not change what it is. Aggregate denial rates are shareable. A denial is not.

notes.title: Write-off authority
notes.content:
Five thousand dollars per account, and the decision is documented against the account.

Above that goes to Finance, which means it goes to someone who should not be reading the clinical detail behind it — so the escalation packet carries the amount and the reason class, never the account.

notes.title: Appeals backlog
notes.content: Two hundred and eleven open, forty of them past the payer's stated response window. The forty are worth chasing as a group rather than individually.

notes.title: Revenue cycle — the shape of it
notes.content:
Registration, coding, billing, payment, denial, appeal. Errors are cheapest to fix at registration and most expensive at appeal.

Everyone focuses on appeals because that is where the pain is visible.

notes.title: Registration accuracy
notes.content:
About 4% of encounters carry an insurance error at registration. Every one becomes a denial forty days later.

The fix is at the front desk, which does not report to me, and the cost lands in my department.

notes.title: Coding — staffing and backlog
notes.content:
Six coders, backlog of seven to twelve days post-discharge.

Two are contract and cost forty percent more. Recruiting permanent coders is hard because the work is remote-friendly and the market is national.

notes.title: Payer mix
notes.content:
Four commercial payers, two government programmes, and self-pay.

Mix has shifted two points toward government over three years, which moves the whole revenue picture and is nobody's decision.

notes.title: Denial categories
notes.content:
Eligibility, authorisation, medical necessity, coding, and timely filing.

Timely filing denials are pure process failure and there is no argument to make. Those are the ones that should be zero and are not.

notes.title: Prior authorisation burden
notes.content:
Two full-time staff doing nothing but authorisations. That is a cost that exists only because the process exists.

Automation helps at the margin. The volume is set by payer policy, not by us.

notes.title: Bad debt and charity care
notes.content:
Policy is generous by sector standards and the board supports it.

The operational difficulty is identifying eligibility early rather than after an account has aged into collections, which is where it currently happens.

notes.title: Price transparency compliance
notes.content:
Machine-readable file published and current. Consumer-facing estimator live.

Usage of the estimator is negligible. Compliance and usefulness turned out to be different projects.

notes.title: Days in accounts receivable
notes.content:
Forty-eight days, down from fifty-three. Sector median is around forty-five.

The improvement is coding backlog, not collections, and I say that explicitly because otherwise the collections team gets credit they did not earn.

notes.title: Appeals — what works
notes.content:
Clinical documentation attached to the first appeal. Second appeals succeed rarely enough that the effort is usually better spent on the next first appeal.

The exception is a systematic denial pattern, where the appeal is really a contract argument.

notes.title: Underpayment recovery
notes.content:
Contract modelling flags payments below expected. Roughly 1.5% of paid claims are underpaid.

Most are small, all are recoverable, and chasing them individually costs more than they are worth, which is why they persist.

notes.title: Revenue cycle — the shape of the operation
notes.content: Fourteen staff across coding, billing, and denials. Roughly 4,200 claims a month.

notes.title: Clean claim rate
notes.content: 87%. The 13% that reject on submission are mostly registration data — wrong plan, expired coverage, name mismatch — and they are fixable at the front desk, not here.

notes.title: Coding accuracy audits
notes.content: Quarterly internal audit, 100 charts. Accuracy 94%. Under-coding is more common than over-coding, which nobody outside revenue cycle believes.

notes.title: Charity care and financial assistance
notes.content: Policy exists, uptake is low, and the reason is that patients do not know it exists until they get a bill they cannot pay.

notes.title: Underpayment identification
notes.content: Contract modelling flags claims paid below the contracted rate. Recovered a meaningful amount last year and it is entirely a function of having the model, not of anyone noticing.

notes.title: Bad debt and collections
notes.content: Sent to an agency after 120 days and three statements. The policy is defensible and it is still the part of this job I like least.

notes.title: Why claims are not a finance dataset
notes.content: Every conversation with someone outside revenue cycle starts here. A claim names a patient, a diagnosis, a service and a provider. Aggregating it makes it reportable; it does not make it not-PHI.

notes.title: Month-end close — revenue cycle side
notes.content: Accruals for unbilled and for expected denials. The denial accrual is a judgement and it is the number Finance queries every month.
